text:
NORA. Tomorrow I am going home—I mean, to my old hometown. It will be easiest for me there to find something or other to do.

HELMER. Oh, you blind, inexperienced creature.

NORA. I must try to gain experience, Torvald.

HELMER. Leave your home, your husband, and your children! And you do not think about what people will say.

NORA. I cannot take that into consideration. I know only that it will be necessary for me.

HELMER. Oh, it is outrageous. That you can betray your most sacred duties in this way.

NORA. What, then, do you consider my most sacred duties?

HELMER. And should I need to tell you that! Are they not your duties toward your husband and your children?

NORA. I have other duties just as sacred.

HELMER. You do not. What duties could those be?

NORA. My duties toward myself.

HELMER. First and foremost, you are a wife and mother.

NORA. I no longer believe that. I believe that first and foremost I am a human being, I, just as much as you are—or at any rate that I must try to become one. I know very well that most people agree with you, Torvald, and that something of the sort is written in the books. But I can no longer be satisfied with what most people say and what is written in the books. I must think these things over for myself and try to understand them.

HELMER. Should you not understand your position in your own home? Do you not have an infallible guide in such matters? Do you not have religion?

NORA. Oh, Torvald, I really do not properly know what religion is at all.

HELMER. What are you saying!

NORA. I know nothing beyond what Pastor Hansen said when I went to confirmation classes. He explained that religion was this and that. When I get away from all this here and am alone, I shall examine that matter too. I shall see whether what Pastor Hansen said was right, or at any rate whether it is right for me.

HELMER. Oh, such a thing is unheard of from so young a woman! But if religion cannot guide you, then at least let me awaken your conscience. Surely you have some moral sense? Or answer me—perhaps you have none?

NORA. Yes, Torvald, that is not easy to answer. I really do not know at all. I am completely at a loss about such things. I know only that I have a very different opinion of such matters from yours. I now hear, too, that the laws are different from what I thought; but that those laws should be right is something I cannot possibly get into my head. So a woman is not to have the right to spare her old, dying father, or to save her husband’s life! I do not believe in such things.

HELMER. You speak like a child. You do not understand the society in which you live.

NORA. No, I do not. But now I intend to learn about it. I must try to find out who is right, society or I.

HELMER. You are ill, Nora; you have a fever; I almost believe you are out of your mind.

NORA. I have never felt so clear and certain as I do tonight.

HELMER. And clear and certain, you are leaving your husband and your children?

NORA. Yes; I am.

HELMER. Then only one explanation is possible.

NORA. Which one?

HELMER. You no longer love me.

NORA. No, that is precisely it.

HELMER. Nora!—And you say that!

NORA. Oh, it hurts me so much, Torvald; for you have always been so kind to me. But I cannot help it. I no longer love you.

HELMER (with forced composure). Is this also a clear and certain conviction?

NORA. Yes, perfectly clear and certain. That is why I do not wish to remain here any longer.

HELMER. And will you also be able to explain to me how I have forfeited your love?

NORA. Yes, I can readily do that. It was this evening, when the wonderful thing did not happen; for then I saw that you were not the man I had imagined you to be.

HELMER. Explain yourself more fully; I do not understand you.

NORA. I have waited so patiently for eight years now; for, dear God, I understood well enough that the wonderful thing does not happen every day. Then this crushing blow came upon me; and then I was infallibly certain: now the wonderful thing will happen. When Krogstad’s letter lay out there, it never once entered my mind that you might be willing to submit to that man’s terms. I was infallibly certain that you would say to him: make the matter known to the whole world. And when that had happened—

HELMER. Yes, and then what? When I had exposed my own wife to shame and disgrace—!

NORA. When that had happened, I thought with infallible certainty that you would step forward and take everything upon yourself and say: I am the guilty one.

HELMER. Nora—!

NORA. You think I would never have accepted such a sacrifice from you? No, of course not. But what would my assurances have counted for against yours?—That was the wonderful thing for which I went on hoping in terror. And it was to prevent it that I wanted to end my life.

HELMER. I would gladly work nights and days for you, Nora—bear sorrow and privation for your sake. But no one sacrifices his honor for the person he loves.

NORA. A hundred thousand women have done so.

HELMER. Oh, you both think and speak like a foolish child.

NORA. Let that be so. But you neither think nor speak like the man to whom I could bind myself. When your fright was over—not at what threatened me, but at what you yourself were exposed to—and when all the danger was past, then for you it was as though nothing at all had happened. I was exactly as before, your little songbird, your doll, whom from then on you would carry in your hands with twice the care, since it was so fragile and frail. (rises.) Torvald—in that moment it dawned on me that for eight years I had lived here with a strange man, and that I had had three children—. Oh, I cannot bear to think of it! I could tear myself to pieces.

HELMER (heavily). I see it; I see it. An abyss has indeed opened between us.—Oh, but Nora, could it not be filled in?

NORA. As I am now, I am no wife for you.

HELMER. I have the strength to become another man.

NORA. Perhaps—if your doll is taken away from you.

HELMER. Oh, to part—to part from you! No, no, Nora, I cannot grasp that thought.

NORA (goes into the room on the right). Then it is all the more certain that it must happen. (she returns with her outer clothing and a small traveling bag, which she sets on the chair by the table.)

HELMER. Nora, Nora, not now! Wait until tomorrow.

NORA (puts on her coat). I cannot spend the night in a strange man’s rooms.

HELMER. But could we not live here as brother and sister—?
